question.prompt:
Consider the figure consisting of a square, its diagonals, and the segments joining the midpoints of opposite sides. The total number of triangles of any size in the figure is

[Figure 1](figures/1995_AMC_12_Q09_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
Let \(O\) be the center of the square. All four drawn interior lines pass through \(O\), so classify triangles according to whether \(O\) is one of their vertices.

[Figure 1](figures/1995_AMC_12_Q09_question_fig1.svg)

For a triangle with vertex \(O\), the opposite side must lie on the square's boundary. Otherwise all three side lines would pass through \(O\) and would not enclose a triangle. On each square side, the two corners and the midpoint give three possible bases: either half of the side or the whole side. Each base has drawn segments joining its endpoints to \(O\). Thus there are
\[
4\cdot 3=12
\]
such triangles. Each is counted once because its side opposite \(O\) is unique.

For a triangle without vertex \(O\), at most one side can lie on an interior line: two distinct interior side lines would meet at \(O\), making \(O\) a vertex. Consequently two sides must lie on adjacent boundary sides of the square. The third side must be a full diagonal, since the midpoint-joining segments connect opposite boundary sides. Each of the two diagonals gives two half-square triangles, for \(2\cdot2=4\) triangles.

Every triangle belongs to exactly one of these cases, so the total is
\[
12+4=\boxed{16},
\]
choice \(\text{D}\).
solutions.title: Separate triangles by whether the center is a vertex
